caption:
Save $100 for your baby. Canada adds $20. In Canada, the RESP grant adds 20% to what you save for a child, but it needs your baby's Social Insurance Number (SIN).

WHY: the Canada Education Savings Grant (CESG) adds 20% on the first $2,500 you put into an RESP each year. That's $20 for every $100, up to $500 a year, with a $7,200 lifetime max. An RESP (Registered Education Savings Plan) is a savings plan for school after high school. To open an RESP, you and the child both need a SIN.

HOW:
1. When you register the birth, tick the box to apply for your baby's SIN (every province offers this; in the territories, apply through Service Canada).
2. Book a meeting with a bank or other RESP provider.
3. Bring your SIN and your baby's SIN, open the RESP, and ask them to apply for the grant.

THE CATCH: no SIN, no RESP, so no grant yet. Missed years aren't all lost: unused grant room carries forward, but you can only catch up a little at a time (at most $1,000 of grant in one year). Grants stop after the year your child turns 17.

WHO THIS IS FOR: kids living in Canada; grants are paid until the end of the year the child turns 17. Parents and grandparents can open the RESP. Lower-income families may also get extra grant money and the Canada Learning Bond.

Do this: get baby's SIN with the birth registration.

Send this to someone who just had a baby.

Education only, not financial advice.

Follow for one money rule a day, in plain words.

#personalfinancecanada #RESP #newparents #canadianmoney #cesg

caption:
One pension? Split it. Pay less tax? In Canada, a retired couple (married or common-law) can split eligible pension income on their tax returns: up to half can be reported by the other spouse.

WHY: Canada's income tax rates rise as income rises. When one person has all the pension income, more of it can land in a higher bracket. Moving up to 50% to the partner with less income can lower the couple's total tax. It's a paper move on the returns; no money changes accounts.

HOW:
1. At tax time, fill in form T1032, Joint Election to Split Pension Income.
2. Both of you sign it, with the same numbers on both copies.
3. Each of you files the same election with your own return by the filing deadline. You can pick a different share each year.

THE CATCH: CPP and OAS don't count. Income from a RRIF counts only once the person with the pension is 65 or older at the end of the year (or after a spouse's death). Workplace pension payments (a life annuity from a pension plan) generally count at any age. You both need to be residents of Canada on December 31 and not separated for 90 days or more because the relationship broke down.

WHO THIS IS FOR: married or common-law couples in Canada, not separated, where one partner gets much more pension income than the other.

Do this: both sign form T1032 at tax time.

Send this to your parents.

Education only, not financial advice.

Follow for one money rule a day, in plain words.

#personalfinancecanada #retirementcanada #CRA #canadianmoney #pensionsplitting

Sources (checked Nov 2 2026):
• CRA, 'Pension income splitting' (canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/tax/individuals/topics/pension-income-splitting.html, modified 2026-01-20): 'You can allocate up to 50% of your eligible pension income to your spouse or common-law partner'; life annuity payments from a pension plan generally qualify; RRIF and annuity amounts qualify if the transferring spouse is 65 or older at the end of the year (or on a spouse's death); old age security and CPP/QPP are not eligible; Form T1032 'must be completed, signed and attached to both' returns, filed by the due date.
• CRA, 'How to split your pension income' (canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/tax/individuals/topics/pension-income-splitting/you-split-your-pension-income.html, modified 2026-01-20): both residents of Canada on December 31; not living apart for 90+ days including Dec 31 because of a breakdown in the relationship; the same percentage isn't required every year.
